profiles.meeting_scenario: A coordination meeting between the infrastructure analytics lead and the data engineering lead for a software engineering research project studying the evolution of GitHub Actions workflows. The team is two weeks away from freezing the dataset for the empirical paper's replication package, and this meeting is meant to align the handoff between the mining pipeline and the analysis notebooks. The agenda is to confirm what the next 'weekly snapshot' will contain, what counts as a 'workflow change history' in the exported tables, how the qualitative labels from the 439-file sample will be attached to the large-scale data, and who will update the shared schema and manifest. The expected outcome is apparent agreement on the export format, ownership of the shared artifacts, and timing for the next handoff so that both workstreams can proceed without blocking each other.

members.name: Nina Park
members.expertise: Repository mining, GitHub API data collection, reproducible data pipelines
members.background: Nina built the ingestion pipeline that collects workflow files and commit-level histories across GitHub repositories and maintains the project's storage layout on the lab cluster.
members.private_state: She wants to avoid rerunning the expensive mining jobs and is trying to keep the export process stable enough to freeze the replication package on schedule; she is also worried that ad hoc schema tweaks from downstream analysis will create provenance problems.
hidden_assumptions: A 'weekly snapshot' means the Monday 00:00 UTC materialized export generated from data already ingested by the end of the previous UTC day.
A 'workflow change history' refers to the lineage of a single physical workflow file path within a repository, not a logical workflow that may move or be renamed.
When analysts ask for the labeled sample to be 'joined in,' they only need repository-level and file-path-level references in a sidecar table, not the labels embedded into the main event table.
The shared manifest is owned by the data engineering side because it is derived from the export job and should only be updated when a new versioned dataset is published.

members.name: Omar Velasquez
members.expertise: Large-scale software repository analysis, statistical reporting, qualitative-to-quantitative coding integration
members.background: Omar leads the analysis notebooks and paper figures, and he previously worked on mining studies where logical entities were tracked across file renames and sample annotations were merged directly into analysis-ready tables.
members.private_state: He wants the handoff to minimize notebook-side data wrangling so he can finalize figures quickly, and he is concerned that subtle inconsistencies in exported entities will force late revisions to counts already drafted in the paper.
hidden_assumptions: A 'weekly snapshot' means the analyst-facing cut for the current reporting week, including all commits observed up to the end of that week in Pacific time because that is how he organizes notebook checkpoints.
A 'workflow change history' refers to the evolution of the same logical workflow across renames or moves, since the research question is about workflow evolution rather than path evolution.
If the qualitative labels are 'joined in,' they will appear directly in the main analysis table at the change-event level so the notebooks can aggregate without extra joins.
The shared manifest is a living coordination document that either workstream can update when they add columns, codebooks, or caveats needed for the paper.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to delivering the next 'weekly snapshot' on Friday.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means she will publish the already-materialized Monday 00:00 UTC weekly export by Friday after validation; the contents are effectively fixed from the prior UTC cutoff.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the Friday handoff will contain data current through the end of that same reporting week, roughly through Friday or week-end in Pacific-time analyst practice.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are discussing coordination timing rather than dataset semantics, and 'weekly snapshot' sounds like a standard internal artifact whose meaning is already shared, so neither thinks to restate the temporal cutoff.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as a workflow change history
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say the export should preserve 'workflow change histories' for the analysis.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 will preserve histories by file path, so a rename from .github/workflows/ci.yml to build.yml starts a new history because the pipeline keys histories by path.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 expects histories to continue across renames or moves when the workflow is logically the same automation, because that is what he believes the study's evolution claims require.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: They agree on the research goal of studying evolution and use the same phrase, but the distinction between physical-path continuity and logical-workflow continuity is second-order and usually buried in implementation details.

misalignment_points.topic: How the labeled sample will be 'joined in'
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree that the 439-file qualitative labels will be 'joined in before analysis'.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 plans to provide a separate sidecar mapping table keyed by repository and file path, expecting Omar's notebooks to join it as needed.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 expects the export job to denormalize the labels directly into the main change-event table so downstream notebooks can treat them as native columns.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: At the coordination level, 'joined in' sounds like a settled implementation detail and both options are standard, so the phrase creates false consensus without prompting a discussion of where the join actually happens.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both mention updating the 'shared manifest' after the handoff.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes the manifest is a versioned export artifact maintained only by the data pipeline owner when a dataset release is cut.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes the manifest is a collaborative working document that he can edit with analysis notes, column interpretations, and caveats as soon as he receives the handoff.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The manifest already exists and both treat it as familiar shared infrastructure, so they discuss 'updating' it without surfacing that they are presupposing different governance and editing norms.
